5.question: Riya saw an old woman carrying two heavy bags. She was getting late for school, but she stopped and helped the woman cross the road. What does Riya's action show?

options.text: She does not care about school.
She values helping someone in need.

5.question: “The classroom buzzed with excitement when the trip was announced.” What does “buzzed” mean here?
Arjun wants to borrow a ruler from a classmate he does not know well. Which is most appropriate?

options.text: Could I please borrow your ruler for a minute?
You must give it to me.

5.question: Meera is writing about yesterday. Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: We visit the museum and see paintings.
We visited the museum and saw paintings.
We will visit the museum and saw paintings.

5.question: Aman entered quietly and lowered the TV volume when he saw his mother sleeping. Why?

options.text: He did not want to disturb her.
She told him to switch it off.

5.question: Choose the best correction: “My sister have two beautiful puppy.”

options.text: My sister has two beautiful puppies.
My sister have two beautiful puppies.
My sister has two beautiful puppy.

5.question: Put these lemonade steps in order: P Add sugar and water. Q Squeeze lemon juice. R Stir well. S Serve.
Notice: “SAVE WATER – Turn off the tap while brushing. Every drop counts!” What is its main purpose?
A boy finds an injured bird, cares for it, and releases it when it can fly. Best title?
A friend suggests leaving picnic wrappers in the park. Best response?

options.text: Let's collect them and use a bin so the park stays clean.

6.question: The school library introduced a 'silent reading hour'. After a month, more students began borrowing books. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.text: The reading hour encouraged interest in books.

6.question: “The little plant struggled through the crack in the pavement.” What does “struggled” suggest?
You disagree with your teammate's idea. Which response is most constructive?

options.text: I see your point; could we also consider this option?
I will not work with you.

6.question: Choose the sentence that best reports a completed action.

options.text: Sara has finished her project yesterday.

6.question: A poster says, “Bring a bottle. Refill. Reuse. Reduce plastic.” Who is the likely target audience?

options.text: People who want to reduce single-use plastic.

6.question: Choose the best connector: “The road was flooded; _____, the match was postponed.”
A character returns a wallet containing money without taking anything. Which trait is best supported?
Which sentence is the clearest instruction?

options.text: Maybe you can perhaps close the door.
Close the door gently before you leave.

6.question: A paragraph gives facts about how bees pollinate flowers. Its main purpose is to:
“Although Tara was nervous, she stepped onto the stage and began her speech.” What can we infer?

7.question: A town replaced some streetlights with solar lamps. Electricity use fell, but cloudy weeks caused problems. Which statement best evaluates the change?

options.text: It saved electricity but needs a backup plan.

7.question: “The principal's announcement sparked a lively debate.” “Sparked” means:
Which sentence uses the most suitable tone for an email to a teacher?

options.text: Could you please share the notes when convenient?

7.question: Choose the best revision: “The team were tired. They continued because they wanted finish the task.”

options.text: The team was tired, but it continued because it wanted to finish the task.
The team tired and continued finish.
The team were tired because finish.

7.question: An advertisement says, “One reusable bottle can replace hundreds of disposable ones.” Its main persuasive technique is:
A story is narrated by a child who misunderstands some adult conversations. Why might the author choose this viewpoint?

options.text: To let readers infer more than the narrator understands.

7.question: Choose the sentence with the clearest cause-and-effect relationship.

options.text: It rained, and books are useful.
Because heavy rain flooded the field, the game was cancelled.
The game was cancelled but rain.

7.question: A student summarizes a 300-word passage by copying 150 words. What should she do instead?

options.text: Select the main ideas and express them briefly in her own words.

7.question: “The room was so quiet that the ticking clock sounded like a drum.” This comparison mainly emphasizes:
Two reports give different figures for the same event. What should a careful reader do first?

options.text: Check the source and date of each report.

8.question: A school bans phones during lessons but allows them for teacher-approved research. What principle does this policy reflect?

options.text: Students cannot be trusted at all.

8.question: “Her argument was compelling because it was supported by evidence.” “Compelling” most nearly means:
Which statement is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: This is the most inspiring novel in the library.

8.question: Choose the best way to combine: “The experiment failed. The students learned from it. They changed the design.”

options.text: The experiment failed, but the students learned from it and changed the design.
The experiment failed the students changed.

8.question: A speech begins with, “Imagine waking up to a city with no clean water.” Why is this opening effective?

options.text: It creates a vivid situation that engages the audience.

8.question: A narrator says, “Of course I wasn't scared,” but then describes trembling hands. What does this suggest?

options.text: The narrator may be hiding fear.

8.question: Which revision removes ambiguity? “Rohan told Arjun that his project was selected.”

options.text: Rohan told Arjun, “Your project was selected.”
Rohan told Arjun his project selected.
His project was selected by his.

8.question: An article gives only advantages of a new rule and ignores all objections. A critical reader should notice:
Which evidence best supports the claim “Reading daily improves vocabulary”?

options.text: A friend says reading is fun.
A study comparing vocabulary growth of regular and infrequent readers.

8.question: A student wants to shorten a paragraph without changing its meaning. Which strategy is best?

options.text: Remove repeated ideas and unnecessary words.
Delete all examples and main ideas.
Replace every word with a longer one.

9.question: A report states that bicycle use rose after new cycle lanes were built. What additional information is most needed before claiming the lanes caused the rise?

options.text: Whether other factors, such as fuel prices or campaigns, also changed.

9.question: “The proposal met with considerable resistance.” “Resistance” here means:
Which sentence is most appropriate in a formal letter to a municipal authority?

options.text: I request that the damaged section of the road be repaired at the earliest convenience.
You guys need to do something.

9.question: Choose the most coherent revision: “The data was collected. The sample was small. The conclusion should be treated cautiously.”

options.text: Because the sample was small, the conclusion drawn from the collected data should be treated cautiously.

9.question: A writer describes a deserted station using words such as “hollow”, “fading”, and “lonely”. What mood is mainly created?
An editorial presents statistics but gives no source. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Accept them because numbers are always objective.
Check whether the statistics come from a credible source.

9.question: Which sentence contains the strongest evidence rather than a general claim?

options.text: A controlled study found improved endurance after eight weeks of regular exercise.

9.question: A character repeatedly avoids answering a direct question. What may this behaviour suggest?
Which is the best summary of a paragraph that gives three examples showing how community gardens improve neighbourhoods?

options.text: Community gardens can benefit neighbourhoods in several ways.

9.question: A headline reads, “Miracle App Guarantees Perfect Marks!” What should a critical reader question first?

options.text: The absolute claim and the evidence behind it.

10.question: A survey of 50 students from one school is used to claim that “all Indian teenagers prefer online learning.” What is the main weakness?

options.text: The sample is too limited to support such a broad claim.

10.question: “The minister's response was deliberately ambiguous.” “Ambiguous” means:

options.text: open to more than one interpretation

10.question: Which thesis is most suitable for an analytical paragraph?

options.text: Urban air pollution requires coordinated action because transport, industry and waste burning all contribute to the problem.

10.question: Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure.

options.text: The programme aims to improve reading, developing confidence, and teamwork.
The programme aims to improve reading, develop confidence, and strengthen teamwork.
The programme aims improving, develop, teamwork.

10.question: A writer quotes only experts who agree with her position. What should a critical reader consider?

options.text: Whether relevant opposing evidence has been omitted.
Whether experts should ever be quoted.

10.question: “He smiled as he signed the resignation letter, but his fingers lingered on the pen.” What is suggested?
Which transition best completes: “The plan is inexpensive. _____, it can be implemented quickly.”
A news report distinguishes clearly between eyewitness statements and confirmed facts. Why is this useful?

options.text: It helps readers separate claims from verified information.
It removes the need for evidence.

10.question: Which revision is most concise? “At this point in time, we are currently unable to make a decision.”

options.text: At this current point, we are unable currently.
We at this time cannot make a decision currently.

10.question: A persuasive essay makes a strong claim but provides only emotional examples. What would improve it most?

11.question: A research article reports a correlation between screen time and poor sleep. Which conclusion is most responsible?

options.text: Screen time definitely causes poor sleep.
The variables are associated, but correlation alone does not prove causation.
Poor sleep causes every use of screens.
The study proves nothing at all.

11.question: “The author's criticism is nuanced rather than absolute.” “Nuanced” means:
Which sentence best maintains an academic tone?

options.text: The findings indicate a significant change in participant responses.

11.question: Choose the most precise revision: “Many things caused the project to fail.”

options.text: Several factors, including inadequate funding and delayed approvals, contributed to the project's failure.

11.question: A memoir is written decades after the events described. What should a critical reader keep in mind?

options.text: Memory may shape or alter details over time.

11.question: A speaker uses a personal story before presenting statistics. What is the likely effect?

options.text: To combine emotional engagement with factual support.

11.question: Two credible sources interpret the same historical event differently. What is the best response?

options.text: Compare their evidence, perspective and reasoning.

11.question: Which sentence avoids a dangling modifier?

options.text: Walking through the corridor, the notice caught Maya's attention.
Walking through the corridor, Maya noticed the poster.
Running quickly, the gate was reached.

11.question: A claim is supported by one dramatic anecdote but contradicted by a large dataset. Which evidence generally deserves greater weight?

options.text: The anecdote because it is memorable.
The large, relevant dataset, while still checking its quality.

11.question: An author repeatedly uses “we” and “our” in a campaign speech. This mainly helps to:

options.text: create a sense of shared identity

12.question: A policy article claims a programme “proved successful” because 80% of participants improved, but gives no control group. What is the strongest limitation?

options.text: Improvement cannot confidently be attributed to the programme without a meaningful comparison.
Eighty is too large a number.
Control groups are only used in literature.

12.question: “The conclusion is plausible but not definitive.” “Definitive” most nearly means:
Which sentence best expresses a qualified academic claim?

options.text: The evidence suggests that excessive social-media use may affect some forms of face-to-face interaction.
Everyone knows social media is bad.
Social media has no effects whatsoever.

12.question: Choose the most effective synthesis of two sources: Source A says remote work increases flexibility; Source B warns it can increase isolation.

options.text: Remote work may increase flexibility while also creating risks of social isolation.
The sources cancel each other out.

12.question: An author describes an opponent's complex argument as “They simply hate progress.” What flaw is most evident?

options.text: The opponent's position has been oversimplified.
The argument uses too much data.

12.question: Which revision is clearest? “The committee discussed the proposal which was controversial for two hours.”

options.text: For two hours, the committee discussed the controversial proposal.
The committee controversial discussed two hours proposal.

12.question: A report funded by a company concludes that the company's product is superior. What should a careful reader do?

options.text: Consider the funding relationship and examine the methods and independent evidence.

12.question: “The city never sleeps” is used in an essay about urban life. This is primarily:
A writer acknowledges a counterargument and then responds with evidence. Why is this often effective?

options.text: It shows awareness of competing views and strengthens the reasoning.
It proves the counterargument is silly.
It eliminates the need for a thesis.

12.question: A viral post quotes one sentence from a long interview. Before judging the speaker, what should a responsible reader do?

options.text: Read the surrounding context and verify the original source.
